title: From San Fernando to ICE: Violence Against Migrants Knows No Borders
author: Diego Torres
content:
_This article by Diego Torres appears in the November 2026 issue of_ Let's
Talk About Migration _(_ Hablemos de Migración _), a magazine on migration
issues published by the Frente Amplio de Mexicanos y Migrantes.[Read and
download the full November
issue](https://diegotorres72.com/internacional/boletin-hablemos-de-
migracion-2/)._

![Let's Talk About Migration](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-
content/uploads/2025/06/image-1.png)

The brutality with which ICE persecutes the migrant community in the United
States is a daily headline in various American and Mexican media outlets.
However, this is not a new phenomenon in the history of migration flows. The
violence with which people are attacked from the moment they are expelled from
their communities until they manage to reach the United States—if they manage
to reach it at all—is a reality that has been unfolding in an increasingly
violent and, also, increasingly publicized manner.

It is necessary to denounce and condemn these acts, but equally important is
remembering that, while we demand justice for those killed by ICE, we must
also demand justice for the migrants who have lost their lives along the way.
In this regard, Mexico has much work to do. Organizations such as Human Rights
Watch have documented how migrants transiting through Mexico face extortion,
kidnapping, and abuse at the hands of organized crime and even authorities,
while containment policies hinder access to safer routes.

The INM, like U.S. immigration authorities, has forced migrants to travel
along increasingly dangerous routes; this has clearly had deadly consequences.
Among these consequences is one of the most violent and grotesque events in
recent migration history: the San Fernando massacre in Tamaulipas.

Between August 22 and 23, 2010, 58 male and 14 female migrants were murdered
in that municipality. The massacre was attributed to the Los Zetas criminal
organization. To date, 63 of the victims have been identified, originally from
Guatemala, Honduras, El Salvador, Ecuador, Brazil, and India, according to the
Foundation for Justice and the Democratic Rule of Law. Diverse nationalities,
but the same pain of having been expelled from their homes. Migrants whose
suffering ended, but not before enduring the terror of kidnapping, torture,
and death, which is now being replicated under different circumstances on the
streets of the United States.

![From San Fernando to ICE: Violence Against Migrants Knows No
Borders](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/ltam-
nov26-04-body-p15.jpg)Illustration: _Let 's Talk About Migration_, November
2026

And just as we denounce the impunity surrounding ICE's actions, those
responsible for these crimes in Mexico have faced years of incomplete
investigations and unresolved justice. The National Human Rights Commission
(CNDH) itself continues to consider the massacre a grave violation of human
rights, while organizations supporting the families have pointed out that many
questions about what happened remain unanswered. The circumstances change, but
the pain they inflict remains the same.

The 72 were kidnapped, just as we see migrants detained today by masked ICE
agents. They were extorted, the little money they or their families were able
to hand over to pay the ransom stolen; just as the U.S. immigration system
strips migrants of their savings in processes that, in many cases, do not
resolve their immigration problem and only prolong their suffering.

They were also used to fuel a criminal enterprise, while in the United States,
immigration detention has become a multi-billion-dollar business for private
companies. Reuters reported that ICE projected spending $38.3 billion in 2026
on expanding and upgrading detention centers. Furthermore, there is court
evidence of detained migrants working for as little as one dollar a day: in
the case of the Tacoma detention center, operated by the GEO Group, a federal
court documented that detainees performed cooking, laundry, cleaning, and
maintenance work for that amount.

The deaths of 72 migrants in San Fernando are not the only instances of
immigrants who have met their end instead of the "American Dream." The
massacre came to light thanks to one of the survivors, who, despite being
shot, managed to reach a Mexican Navy checkpoint and report what had happened.
The National Human Rights Commission (CNDH) itself documented this event in
its investigation of the case.

![From San Fernando to ICE: Violence Against Migrants Knows No
Borders](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/ltam-
nov26-04-body-p16.jpg)Illustration: _Let 's Talk About Migration_, November
2026

But in Mexico, there are hundreds of clandestine graves where unidentified
bodies lie, and among them may be migrants who may never be searched for by
the government, leaving the search to the mothers who are searching for their
missing loved ones. The San Fernando massacre itself demonstrated the
magnitude of the problem: months after the massacre of the 72, 193 bodies were
found in clandestine graves in that same municipality. The difficulty in
identifying the victims and linking them to missing people hidden a portion of
the true human cost of migration routes.

Another similarity to this case is the pronouncements of human rights
organizations that serve to become headline news and then are lost due to the
incapacity of the Mexican government and the indifference of the US
government, sending a clear signal to the whole world: migrants are not a
priority.

Furthermore, violence against migrants was widely reported before San
Fernando. Since 2009, a year before the massacre, the National Human Rights
Commission had documented the existence of mass kidnappings of migrants in
Mexico. In an investigation conducted between September 2008 and February
2009, 198 kidnapping incidents were recorded, affecting 9,758 people. In other
words, the Mexican state had information about the magnitude of the problem
and the extreme vulnerability of those crossing the country.

For his part, Trump's repressive actions against the immigrant community also
had visible precedents dating back to his first term. His "zero tolerance"
policy led to the separation of thousands of families. The Inspector General
of the Department of Homeland Security himself concluded that the government
was unprepared to implement this policy, that minors were detained for
extended periods in facilities designed for short stays, and that there were
serious problems identifying and reuniting families. It was known that these
actions could escalate during his second term as his anti-immigrant rhetoric
hardened. In March 2026, the United Nations Committee on the Elimination of
Racial Discrimination even warned about the "derogatory and dehumanizing"
language used against migrants and noted that portraying them as criminals or
a burden could fuel discrimination and hate crimes.

As we can see, actions against migrants occur on both sides of the border.
These actions have a long history, and the violence used against them
continues to cause deaths. The 72 migrants cowardly murdered in San Fernando
are just a fraction of the enormous number of people who continue to lose
their lives on migration routes around the world.

![From San Fernando to ICE: Violence Against Migrants Knows No
Borders](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/ltam-
nov26-04-body-p19.jpg)Illustration: _Let 's Talk About Migration_, November
2026

And the current figures in the United States also compel us to look in that
direction. As of early October 2026, 58 people had died in ICE custody or
during immigration operations since the beginning of Trump's second term. On
October 19, following the death of Emiliano Andrade Covarrubias at an ICE
processing center in Laredo, Texas, the Mexican Ministry of Foreign Affairs
confirmed that 18 Mexicans had died in custody or during immigration
operations since January 20, 2025.

The pain of migrant families losing their loved ones is immense, regardless of
who the perpetrator was. But it's important to distinguish the nature of the
funding in both cases. ICE operates directly with public funds approved by the
U.S. Congress; in fact, legislation passed in 2025 allocated tens of billions
of additional dollars to immigration detention.

In the case of Mexican organized crime, it cannot be stated that the U.S.
government directly financed Los Zetas. What is documented, however, is the
economic and material relationship that exists with the United States: Mexican
criminal organizations obtain part of their income from the U.S. drug market
and receive weapons trafficked illegally from that country. The U.S.
Government Accountability Office documented that approximately 70% of the
weapons recovered in Mexico and sent for tracing between 2009 and 2014
originated in the United States.

The difference isn't so vast; they simply present themselves differently:
organized crime obtains resources through illicit markets, while ICE 's
funding has been openly approved with public funds by the U.S. Congress. But
in the end, for the families who lose a migrant, no budgetary, political, or
criminal explanation can lessen the pain of a life that will never return. And
worse still, there's no end in sight to the suffering of migrants. Because
behind every migrant who dies, there is a shattered family, a life that could
have been saved, and a responsibility that cannot go unpunished.
